column2: Two Million Views, Eleven Pounds: A Year Inside the Creator Economy
媒体网络
从厨房手机拍摄到百万播放:一位半职视频博主关于流量算法、变现、赞助与倦怠的诚实账本。
B2

I started the channel for the least glamorous reason available: my sourdough starter was overflowing and I needed somewhere to put the enthusiasm. Two years later I have two million cumulative views, forty thousand subscribers, an inbox that sorts itself into brands, scams and fellow bakers, and a monthly income that would not cover my rent in a city I would not want to live in anyway. This is the honest ledger nobody films: the creator economy looks like a lottery from the outside and feels like a smallholding from the inside — endless labour, modest yields, occasional weather.

The first thing the algorithm taught me is that it is not a wizard but a matchmaker. Videos succeed when they are watched, saved and shared, and it measures those signals with unsentimental precision. My breakthrough was accidental: a livestream of a failed bake, left running out of laziness, outperformed every polished upload I had agonised over, because people could write comments in real time and I could laugh at the disaster in real time. Since then I have structured everything around the comment section as a venue rather than an afterthought: asking genuine questions in the first minute, pinning the best reply, letting the audience steer the next episode. The lesson is unglamorous but repeatable — retention is a relationship, not a hook.

Monetisation arrived in tiers, each with its own psychology. Advertising revenue was the first and smallest: eleven pounds in my opening month, a sum so comic I framed the statement. Affiliate links did better, because baking equipment is something people genuinely buy, and honesty turned out to be the strategy — the single highest-earning video I ever made was titled "Do not buy the expensive one", which is not a sentence traditional marketing would survive. A newsletter became the stable spine of the income: people who will follow a recipe across inboxes will follow it anywhere, and an email list, unlike a follower count, cannot be taken away by a redesign.

Sponsorship taught me the hardest lessons. The first offer arrived with flattering speed and a contract written in a language I did not yet speak; I signed it, and spent a fortnight promoting a flour brand I did not use, watching my own comment section cool towards me with every upload. It paid three months of groceries and cost something harder to price. The rules I extracted, expensively: only promote what you already buy; say the price of your integrity out loud and then add VAT; and disclose everything, always, not because regulations require it (they do) but because audiences forgive commerce and punish disguise. A good sponsorship now feels less like an advertisement and more like a collab — the brand sends the ingredient, the audience gets the recipe, and the video would exist anyway.

The costs that surprised me were not financial. Binge-watch culture expects presence in bulk, and the publishing treadmill — edit on Tuesday, film on Thursday, answer comments forever — quietly colonises the week. My burnout arrived not as exhaustion but as numbness: filming a loaf I did not care about, in a kitchen I had stopped seeing, for an audience I had started to fear disappointing. The recovery was structural, not spiritual: fewer videos, prepared in monthly batches; a co-editor paid properly; two comment sessions a week instead of a permanent vigil; and a private account, followed by eleven people, where I post bakes that exist only because I wanted to eat them. The channel survived the retreat, which taught me the year's most valuable lesson: the audience was never asking for volume. The metrics were.

Would I recommend the smallholding? To anyone who wants a craft with a public, absolutely; to anyone who wants a salary, not yet, and possibly never. The two million views were not a jackpot but a slow compounding of usefulness. The eleven pounds is framed and hanging in the kitchen, next to the first loaf photograph and the printout of the first kind comment from a stranger in Chile. Keep the ledger honest, price your integrity with VAT, batch your labour, protect the private joy — and let the algorithm matchmake while you, contentedly, keep baking.
